doc.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995

title: Advice for students and Basie's no bebop drums request
summary: Play softly with intensity, earn respect of other musicians, and Basie's request not to play bebop drums in his swing band.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well in many ways, be kind and have compassion to the other players on the bandstand playing other instruments, especially if you’re a drummer. Because a lot of trumpet players might blow their chops or if you’re playing too loudly behind a singer or something like that. Learn to play and generate dynamic intensity at a soft volume. And that will dedicate you to developing control and that will determine your personality behind your instrument. And I really feel that if people will permit the groove to breathe — one thing that Basie said to me, that I quoted him in my Down Beat article, that he came up to me one night and he said, “Please do me a favor.” And I said, “Anything you want, Chief.” And he says, “Please don’t play bebop drums in my swing band.” In other words, make all your fills self-explanatory. Don’t make — you have to gain the trust of the other musicians you’re attempting to create music and accompany. And if you can gain the respect of the other instrumentalists — you know they usually say, “Oh yeah, it’s fourteen guys and a drummer.” So drummers have to really earn the respect of the other instrumentalists. And I think by drummers just gaining more understanding of the form of the music and learning to help the soloists be inspired to create — you know the utmost compliment that I can be bestowed, is when a soloist will come up to me and say, “Man, thanks for laying down the groove, I needed to tell my story.” I’m not here to play duets with horn players, I’m here to lift them up and give them such a wonderful joyous feeling to play. And if they can relate their story to the people, and then they come up to you and say, “Hey man thanks for laying down the groove,” that’s the greatest compliment in the world to me. So just love the groove, and keep the grin on the groove as much as you can, and aim the beat at their feet, and just hope for the best.
